newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian deputy PM faces new court investigation.
newsitem.headline: Belgian deputy PM faces new court investigation.

text.p: A Belgian parliamentary commission decided early on Thursday to recommend to parliament that deputy prime minister Elio Di Rupo should not be brought before a court to face allegations he had had sex with minors.

Commission chairman Raymond Langendries told reporters that the 11-member body, made up of representatives from the main political parties, instead wanted the Cour de Cassation, the nation's highest court, to investigate the allegations further and to submit a report by December 9 at the latest.
A full session of parliament now must vote on the recommendation. A debate preceeding the vote is expected to be held later on Thursday at a time still to be announced.
Di Rupo, 45 and a discreet homosexual, insists that he has only ever had sex with consenting adults. Homosexuality is not a crime in Belgium. Sex with children younger than 16 is.

The commission made its recommendation after a marathon meeting which began on Wednesday morning and at which it discussed a confidential peadophilia dossier submitted to parliament by the Brussels public prosecutor.
Committee chairman Langendries said a majority of the panel had voted in favour of a continuation of the investigation.
It heard from the prosecutor and Di Rupo in person.
Members of the four parties forming Belgium's ruling coalition meanwhile said that Di Rupo could stay in his job while the new court investigation was under way.
"For me personally I see no reason to tell Di Rupo that he must resign," commission member Tony Van Parys, a member of the Flemish christian democrat CVP party, told reporters.
The CVP is the largest party in the centre-left coalition.

"The prosecutor general's report was not complete enough to warrant lifting Di Rupo's immunity and refer him to court," commission member Renaat Landuyt, a member of the Flemish SP socialist party, told Reuters.
He added that as far as he was concerned Di Rupo did not have to resign. "It would be very unfortunate if Mr Di Rupo would have to resign at this stage," he said.

Asked whether Di Rupo could remain at work pending the court report, commission member Serge Moureaux, like Di Rupo a francophone socialist, said: "The case against Di Rupo is not complete enough to warrant an immediate resignation."
The francophone socialist party is the second biggest in the coalition.
Opposition politicians stopped short of calling for Di Rupo's immediate resignation, but questioned his ability to function normally in the coming weeks.

"It is up to Di Rupo to decide whether he remains in function. But I do not see how he can fulfil his ministerial duties while being under investigation," said commission member Didier Reynders of the opposition francophone liberal party PRL.

The allegations, following an unrelated paedophile sex and murder scandal that has shaken Belgium for the past three months, have further eroded already weak public confidence in the political and judicial system and shaken the government.
